TEXAS MOB HUNTS DOWN
AND KILLS 25 NEGROES
Sheriff Finds There Was No Real
Cause for Slaying the
Black Men
PALESTINE, Texas, July 31.—At least fifteen, and it may be twenty-five, all of them negroes and unarmed, were hunted down and killed by a mob of from 200 to 300 men in the Slocum and Denison Springs neighborhood last night and yesterday, according to the opinion of Sheriff Black today.

The sheriff returned early this morning after twenty-four hours in the district. He told of a fierce man hunt in the woods, of riddled bodies found on lonely roads and of the terror almost indescribable among the inhabitants in the southeastern part of Anderson county.

"I found the greatest excitement prevailing throughout the section of the county," said the sheriff. "Men were going about killing negroes as fast as they could find them, and so far as I have been able to ascertain, without any real cause. These negroes have done no wrong that I could discover. There was just a hot-headed gang hunting them down and killing them. "I believe the trouble was due to a controversy over a promissory note."
alex-holly-palestine-1910-07-29.A6:
From the best information obtainable today, and what seems to be entirely reliable information, the situation in the southeastern part of the county is now thoroughly under control and there seems to be no further danger of trouble. Officers returning from the scene of the trouble confirm the report that ten negroes are known to be dead, but it is emphatically denied that any white men have been injured or killed. The officers also deny that there was at any time a pitched battle between the races, but that it was a pot-shot occasion, in which the above number of negroes were killed.

The arrival of the officers with the state rangers and the fact that a company of militia and one of cavalry were on the ground in Palestine ready to assist the state in preserving order have had a very beneficial effect in giving confidence to the people of the city and county. In conversation with District Judge Gardner this morning a Herald man was informed by him that the bringing of the rangers and troops was a move to restore peace and quiet and not in apprehension of further or more serious trouble.

Four Men Under Arrest.

Last evening about 8 o'clock a detachment of officers arrived in the city having under arrest four white men of this county, and they were locked up on a charge of murder. The men arrested are John Spurger, Wallace Ferguson, Josh Bishop and Tom Garnet. Other arrests are expected today.

Palestine, Tex., Aug. 1.—Ten white men were arrested to-day and placed in jail charged with being implicated in the mob violence in the southern part of this county during the last three days, in which many negroes were slaughtered. Sheriff Black, who has returned from a visit to the scene of bloodshed, said today:

"We will not find all of the bodies until the location is revealed to us by the buzzards. I found the greatest excitement prevailed throughout that section of the country. Men were going about and killing negroes as fast as they could find them, and, so far as I have been able to ascertain, without any real excuse at all. These negroes have never done anything that I could discover. There was just a hot-headed gang hunting them down and killing them.

Find Eleven Bodies.

"We found eleven bodies, but from what I have heard, the dead must number fifteen or twenty. We came across four bodies in one house in a marsh between Denson Springs and Slocum. I understand that Mrs. George Scarborough, of Slocum, saw a party of forty or fifty go through her field. Some of them cut the wire fence and went through on horseback and some of them walked through.

"They went across to the house, where we found the four bodies. One negro had been killed at this house the night before, and three were sitting up with the body, one of them being old and white-haired. These three were not armed.

"I sent two deputies out through the country to collect all the arms they could find in the houses of the negroes. They made a thorough search, but found only nine little single-barreled shotguns, none of which seemed to have been fired lately, and about thirty shells, all loaded with small shot. I am led to believe that the start of the trouble was due to a controversy over a promissory note.

Hunted Like Sheep.

"I think the most of that crowd of men came from Houston, and, according to what I am told, the shooting was still going on late yesterday evening. They were just hunting the negroes down like sheep. We found two deputies out through the country to collect all the negroes were not armed.

MURDER IN TEXAS.
The average "race w
The average "race war" is a one-sided affair in the United States, the killed and wounded being negroes in almost every instance. Some white man engages in an altercation with a negro. The latter holds up his end of the argument as best he can, and his opponent occasionally gets the worst of it. Then the trouble begins.

The most recent outbreak was at Slocum, Texas, where from fifteen to twenty black men were killed in cold blood by a mob of from 200 to 300 white men. The negroes were unarmed and the killing was easy.

The report of the sheriff is calculated to make the blood of a law-abiding citizen run cold. Upon his return from the scene of the murders, he told "of a fierce man hunt in the woods, of riddled bodies found on lonely roads, and of the terror almost indescribable on the part of the inhabitants."

According to the story of the officer, men were going about killing negroes as fast as they could find them and without just cause or provocation, the trouble originating over a promissory note, a black man and a white man being principals in the dispute.

Surely a dispute over the payment of a promissory note was slight cause for the ruthless slaughter of a score of human beings. Why send missionaries to the remote corners of the earth while so much remains to be done in Texas?

Three Soldiers Are Killed.
When the negroes, who had thrown up breastworks of logs and underbrush in the forest about their settlements, saw the troops approaching they opened fire. Three soldiers fell at the first volley, and the negroes were forced by the rush of the troops to retreat to a second line of defense they had constructed.

The first rush of the soldiers was accomplished during this morning, and after its fatal results the troops withdrew to determine, if possible, the strength of the negroes. Again in the afternoon the troops made an attempt to invest the fortifications of the negroes, aided by a detail of planters in the vicinity of Palestine and Jacksonville.

The planters' detachment was assigned to attack one side of the negro stronghold, while the detachment of troop, stormed another. For some reason the negroes chose to direct their fire against the planters, and in the fire eleven were killed outright. After this attack darkness fell and the troops and planters withdrew from the attack.

It is said tonight that 500 fresh men and troops are being rushed to Palestine to engage in an attack on the negro stronghold early Sunday morning.

AUST4N, Tex., July 30—Governor Campbell today ordered a detachment of rangers and a company of State militia to the vicinity of Palestine to quell the race riot which broke out early today.

All Saloons Are Closed.

Judge D. H. Gardner has closed all saloons in the county and city. The saloons will remain closed until conditions warrant reopening. An order was issued by the court forbidding the sale or rental of guns and ammunition for the present. Most of the dealers had already sold out of guns and ammunition.

The negroes of that section have been preparing for trouble and were heavily armed. The whites say they have been very insolent. The negroes at secret meetings at a little schoolhouse near Slocum planned to burn several houses of the white farmers. The plot was given away by one old negro, and as the negroes were on their way to a meeting last night four of them were killed.

The area affected by the trouble is about fifteen miles square, and is in a portion of the county inhabited largely by negroes, and very inaccessible. Tonight at 7 o'clock three State rangers arrived here, and a company of State militia arrived from Marshall.

Speaking editorially of the Slocum, Texas, massacre, the Cleveland Dally Plain Dealer (Dem.) had the following to say in its closing paragraph, and it is so true that we deem it worthy of reproduction in The Gazette: "The reports of 'race wars,' analyzed down as this one has been, would not infrequently disclose a similar state of affairs than massacres of Negroes most of them innocent and offensive. 'Race war,' however, is a handy and high sounding designation, and it may be used at any time to give respectability and a semblance of justification to the killings. Evidently this latest 'race war' in Texas has been an affair of more than usual viciousness, for the authorities are not wont to make much ado over the ordinary clash between 'whites' and blacks in which the former do the killing and the latter are killed." The one encouraging thing in connection with this terrible butchery is the fact that a number of reputable and leading "white" men of that town and vicinity have been found who are willing and ready to go before the grand jury and testify to the barbaric brutality of the Slocum mob. May God see to it that all guilty are punished as such brutal murderers should be, promptly and fully. Recently several of our ladies have said that they have been refused service in the restaurant of Kresge's five and ten cent store on Euclid Avenue, near the Public Square. As we have so often told our readers, there is a way to stop this sort of thing and we presume it will be when our people get enough of it. How so many can quietly submit to such aggravating insults in public places, is more than we can understand. It is no use to tell your troubles to others, but employ a good lawyer and vindicate your rights in the proper place (the courts) and manner. SEVEN MEN ARE INDICTED ON CHARGE OF MURDER AS RESULT OF DEATH OF FIVE NEGROES IN THE SOUTHERN PART OF COUNTY THE LAST OF JULY. REPORT OF GRAND JURY Indorses the Action of Officers For Prompt and Efficient Services Rendered —Believe Sending of State Troops Was Very Wise.
Twenty-two charges of murder in the first degree presented in five indictments covering the killing of five negroes in Anderson county returned against seven white men was the result of the grand jury investigation of the Slocum killings as made public late Wednesday afternoon.

The names of six of the white men covered by these indictments are as follows:

Jim Spurger.
B. J. Jenkins.
Curtis Spurger.
Isom Garner.
Steve Jenkins.
Andrew Kirkwood.

Of these Jim Spurger is indicted in two cases, B. J. Jenkins in four cases, Curtis Spurger in three cases, Isom Garner in four cases, Steve Jenkins in three cases, and Andrew Kirkwood in three cases.

The six men named above are now under arrest, and confined in the county jail. The seventh man indicted has not as yet been arrested, and the authorities withhold his name.

All of the white men now held indicted for Anderson county killings, with the exception of Curtis Spurger, are also charged with the killing of one negro in Houston county. Examining trials will be held in Houston county next week, the grand jury of that county not being in session until October.

These defendants, and possibly others, will be carried to Crockett, Houston county, Monday, for examining trials, for the killing of Will Burley, colored, which occurred in that county. District Attorney Harris will conduct the examinations before a justice of the peace down there, and it is expected further indictments will result from this examination.

The grand jury in making its report to District Judge B. H. Gardner yesterday afternoon about 6 o'clock, touching upon the recent trouble between whites and blacks in the Slocum and Denson Springs communities, used the following language:

"We find that seven negroes were killed in Anderson county and one in Houston county, on or about the 29th, 30th or 31st of July, 1910, and that no white men were killed or injured. We indorse the action of the officers for their prompt and efficient services rendered in the regrettable state of affairs that recently existed in our midst, and after having had witnesses before us by the hundreds and being in position to judge of the state of their minds during the trouble, believe that the services rendered by the state in sending troops was very wise, and did more to quiet the minds of the people than the lack of them would have done. We feel that the rangers have done exceedingly valuable services, as well as to stop flying and exciting rumors instigated by a few men. Our district attorney, T. J. Harris, has had the situation under a complete system of investigation, and he and Mr. John A. Mobley are thoroughly familiar with same in all its details."

Blood Thirsty Butchers
Innocent Colored People Butchered. (Special to The Bee.) Palestine, Tex, Aug. 17, 1910. Editor of the Washington Bee: On reading your issue for August 13, noted a wildly exaggerated statement of the "Negro Massacre" in this county, near Palestine. I beg to state that the source of news in your section of the country has almost entirely spread reports that have never occurred. Being interested in my race and race affairs, I shall give you a sketch of the massacre, knowing the particulars of the barbarism. Near the village of Slocum, in the southeastern part of the county, was the scene of one of the most heinous crimes committed in this section of the country since the Indians. Men (colored men) were shot down like dogs; youths were not spared—whites armed to slaughter chased Negro men in the forest and shot them down wherever they found them. Civilized white men, men of chivalry and honor, took the lives of men who raised not a hand for protection, without any just cause. Some of the incidents are as follows: Two youths were on their way to feed stock when they met a crew of white horsemen, who, without a word, fired upon the youths, wounding them unto death. Three victims seated around the corpse of a dead man, one an old gray-haired gentleman, was killed. After two days of raging, eight Negroes were dead and not one white. Rangers were dispatched to the scene and quieted the riot. They began to investigate the community, as the report had been spread that Negroes were heavily armed, and were fighting a pitched battle with the whites. In the houses of the Negroes was found several single-barrel shotguns. Their muzzles were choked with spider webs, and hadn't been used since squirrel time last fall. Not one was loaded. I notice a report in your paper that the Negroes looted the hardware stores for ammunition. After the rumor of the riot not a Negro was sold ammunition. The looting was wholly untrue. The Negroes were peaceable and raised not an arm towards looting. No soldiers were killed—they didn't go to the scene of the riot, but kept peace at Palestine. AN ORDERLY LYNCHING. Southerners in certain localit
Southerners in certain localities now insist upon the elevated social tone of their lynching parties, says the Springfield Republican. A newspaper correspondent, having wantonly described a certain Mississippi mob as composed of ruffians, has been sharply rebuked by Tax Assessor Miller of Concordia Parish, La., which is just across the river from the place where the lynching took place. Mr. Miller's letter deserves a place in the history of lynching in America, for he writes:—

"The lynching of Elmo Curl at Mastodon, Miss., last night was a most orderly affair, conducted by the bankers, lawyers, farmers and merchants of that county. The best people of the county, as good as there are anywhere, simply met there and hanged Curl without a sign of rowdyism. There was no drinking, no shooting, no yelling and not eveen any loud talking. All of the best people of that section took part, and I have never seen a more orderly assemblage anywhere.

tom-hayes-gantt-1910-07-31.A1:
NEGRO RUSHED TO COUNTY JAIL Charged With Murder of Watchmen. COVINGTON CITIZENS ANGERED Deputy Hastens With Prisoner to Montgomery. IN AUTOMOBILE HE RUSHES TO GANTT, WHERE HE TAKES TRAIN FOR CAPITAL CITY WITH PRISONER.
Andalusia, July 31.—(Special.)—Followed by an ever increasing crowd of anygry men, Deputy Sheriff J. M. Johnson raced in an automobile to the railroad station at Gantt, nine miles from this place, with Tom Hayes, a negro accused of the murder of Night Watchman Sowell of the Empire Lumber Company. The killing took place early Sunday morning, but the body was not discovered until late this morning when the day watchman of the place came on duty.

The body was found with a knife stuck in the throat of the victim, and the ground showed that Sowell had fought for a long time before being overcome. The negro was found at his home by Sheriff Presswood, and offered no resistance to arrest.

Upon the discovery of the body of Sowell, the mill operatives became enraged. The knife was thought to belong to the negro Hayes, and the crowd started after him. Sheriff Presswood was ahead of the crowd, and it was only through the use of the automobile that he was able to keep his prisoner from the hands of the crowd which seemed bent upon lynching.

The country surrounding Andalusia is much excited, and Sheriff Presswood thought it best to keep the negro in the Montgomery County jail until his trial.

Sowell was a young man about thirty-five years old, and bore a good reputation. Hayes is said to have been charged on two occasions with violations of the liquor laws of the state, and had been discharged some time ago from the employ of the Empire Lumber Company. The motive of the killing is not known.

Deputy Sheriff Johnson with his prisoner arrived in Montgomery shortly after 7 o'clock Sunday night. At the jail Hayes was asked why he killed Sowell, and the negro replied that he did not kill him. He would not talk of the affair.

NEGROES ARE SHOT DOWN

TEXAS SHERIFF TELLS STORY OF CARNAGE.

Declares Members of Mob Were Filled With Lust for Blood and Shot Down Negroes Indiscriminately.

Palestine, Tex., July 31.—At least fifteen, and it may be twenty, negroes, all of them probably unarmed, were hunted down and killed by a mob numbering perhaps 200 or 300 men, in the Slocum and Denison Springs neighborhood of Palestine last night and yesterday, according to the opinion of Sheriff Black, expressed today.

The sheriff returned early this morning after a twenty-four-hour absence in that district, where racial trouble has been acute, and described in some detail the conditions which he found to exist there. He told of a fierce man hunt in the woods, of riddled bodies found on lonely roads, and of the terror almost indescribable among the inhabitants in the Southeastern part of Anderson County. Sheriff Black is sure that his estimate of the dead is conservative. He said he had made a careful investigation and after telling of its results, added this statement:

"We won't find some of the bodies until the location is revealed to us by the buzzards.

"I found the greatest excitement prevailing throughout that section of the country. Men were going about and killing negroes as fast as they could find them, and so far as I have been able to ascertain, without any real cause at all. These negroes had never done anything that I could discover. There was just a hot-headed gang hunting them down and killing them.

"We found eleven dead bodies, but from what I have heard the dead must number fifteen or twenty. We came across four bodies in one house.

"I don't know how many there were in the mob, but I think there must have been two or three hundred. I understand that Mrs. George Scarborough of Closum saw a party of forty or fifty go through her field.

"I am led to believe that the main trouble was due to a controversy over a promissory note. This may not be true, but that is the impression I have at this stage of the investigation. R. Alford, a white man who is a cripple, had gone on a negro's note. The note came due and he got after the negro to renew it, or pay, or something of the kind, and the negro would not do it, and cursed him. The incident caused bad feeling.

Places Dead at Fifteen.

"If reports that I have given to me are to be credited, there must be fifteen or twenty dead, all of them negroes. It will be difficult to find out just how many were killed, because the dead are scattered all over the woods. Some probably will never be found."

Although every possible effort has been made by the Anderson County authorities, Adjutant-General Newton, Captain Rogers and two or more rangers who arrived this morning, besides others, are lending their aid to the work. Palestine tonight has very little definite information about the trouble between the whites and blacks between Anderson and Denison Springs. Sunday has been characterized by the utter absence of anything authoritative from there except the report which Sheriff Black made on his return at an early hour this morning.

Judge H. B. Garner received a telephone message from Elkhart this afternoon, which purports to come from Captain G. R. Fowler, who is at the

head of a force of special officers in that county. This message was to the effect that everything was quiet and that the troops would not be needed. The man who sent the message informed Judge Gardner that it had been given to him by Captain Fowler with instructions to bring it to Elkhart and transmit it to Palestine.

"I have received a message from Grapeland," said Judge Gardner, "stating that a negro had been killed near Priscilla this morning, and that the parties engaged in it were hunting another negro for the purpose of killing him. They thought something ought to be done to stop it. I have been trying to find out something about the situation, but when I got in touch with Priscilla, I could not find the officer there. I did talk with some man there who said there had been several negroes killed, but he did not indicate what had been done today. Perhaps it is a part of the other trouble.

"Although there was nothing definite, I sent down two additional automobiles this evening with District Attorney Harris, Captain Rogers of the rangers and three or four men. The purpose is to ascertain the situation and advise me as soon as possible.

"The trouble is practically at an end. We are now trying to fix the responsibility and apprehend the guilty parties. I have been informed that one white man has been arrested, and that he is to be brought here. The grand jury will commence work tomorrow afternoon at 2 o'clock. The bailiffs I have sent down into that county are summoning practically everybody. This is for the two-fold purpose of getting the people out of the county, that order may be restored and of obtaining from them such evidence as they may be able to give."

Adjutant-General Newton accompanied by Captain Rogers of the rangers, Col. R. H. Beckham, assistant quartermaster in the Adjutant-General's department, and two members of the Texas Rifle team of 1910, who are scheduled to be in the national shoot at Camp Perry, Ohio, arrived in Palestine this morning from Austin.

EMPLOYE AT FOSHEE & M'GOURIN MILL AT ANDALUSIA IS KILLED BY TOM HAYES, A NEGRO.
Special to the Journal.

Andalusia, Ala., August 1.—Mr. Sowell, night watchman at the Foshee & McGowan mill here, was killed Saturday night by Tom Hayes, a "blind tiger" negro, who lives near the mill. Mr. Sowell's head was cut nearly off and he was dragged a short distance and hid. He was found at 10 o'clock Sunday and Hayes was arrested by the sheriff and taken in an automobile to Gant station, where the Central train was caught and Hayes was taken on to Montgomery to prevent mob violence.

It was only the precaution of the sheriff that saved the negro. Sowell was a witness against Hayes for selling whiskey.

TAKE NEGRO TO DANGER ZONE TOM HAYES RETURNED TO ANDA- LUSIA, WHERE IT IS VERY PROB- ABLE HE WILL BE LYNCHED. By Associated Press.
Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 22.—When officers took Tom Hayes, a negro, back to Andalusia today he was ushered into a danger zone that holds not more than half a chance for him to escape mob wrath. Hayes confesses that he killed a white man at a saw mill.

Holding his victim's head under his left arm, he cut his throat with his right, leaving the knife imbedded in the flesh of his neck where it was found. When he washed his undershirt in the jail after being rushed here at the time of the tragedy to save him from lynching, blood covered the bottom of a big tub.

FLORIDA RAILROAD IS INCORPORATED IN ALABAMA

By Associated Press.

Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 22.—The incorporation of the Alabama, Florida & Southern railroad to run twenty-five miles from Marmill, Ala., to Malone, Fla., is today reported to the secretary of state. The capital is $40,000, all paid in.
tom-hayes-gantt-1910-07-31.A9:
SHERIFF FOILS PLANS OF MOB Brings Prisoner to Montgomery County Jail. MEN ANGERED BY MURDER Troops Called to Protect Prison at Andalusia. SCOUTING PARTY FROM MOB ARRIVES AT JAIL, BUT FACES LINE OF STEEL NEGRO RUSHED AWAY.
Fearing that another attempt to lynch Tom Hayes, a negro, accused of the murder of Night Watchman R. D. Sowell, at the Empire Lumber Company's yard near Andalusia several weeks ago would be made, Sheriff Prestwood of Andalusia Thursday brought Hayes to the Montgomery county jail for safe keeping, following an attempt by a mob of 250 men Wednesday night to lynch the negro.

Upon the discovery that Sowell had been murdered, Hayes was arrested and placed in jail at Andalusia. Shortly after he was locked up, Sheriff Prestwood received word that an attempt would be made to lynch the prisoner and he was brought here for safe keeping. While here, he is said to have confessed to the brutal murder of Sowell. He is said to have admitted that he held his victim's head under one arm, using his free arm to rip the white man's throat.

Several days ago he was taken back to Andalusia as it was thought feeling against him there had died down. This proved not to be the case, however, as on Tuesday night, the night after Hayes was taken back to Andalusia, Sheriff Prestwood says he had information that a mob was going to attempt to storm the jail and lynch Hayes. Sheriff Prestwood notified the commanding officer of the local militia company of what he had heard and the soldiers were held in readiness to protect the jail at a moment's notice. Nothing happened Tuesday night, however, and the militia disbanded.

Wednesday night Sheriff Prestwood was informed that a mob of 250 men had organized several miles from town and was to storm the jail at 2 o'clock Thursday morning. After ascertaining that the mob really intended to storm the jail, Sheriff Prestwood ordered out the militia company and the jail was surrounded by a strong body of soldiers. Several hours later about twenty-five or thirty members of the mob came to Andalusia, evidently to reconnoiter. Upon finding the jail protected, they immediately left the city and nothing more was heard from the mob.

Hayes was brought here on the first train leaving Andalusia and probably will be kept here until his trial is held.

— Chester special of August 29, to the News and Courier: In the presence of a large assemblage from all parts of the county, the funeral of Jesse H. Hardin, the highly esteemed citizen, faithful Confederate soldier, and successful farmer, were held at Cavalry Baptist church at noon today by Rev. S. R. Brook of Lowryville. An honorary escort of eighteen Confederate soldiers attended the impressive occasion. Senator Allen Johnstone, chairman of Clemson college trustees, and Profs. Stackhouse and Martin of the Clemson faculty were present. The whole of Mr. Hardin's long and active life was spent in the bounds of Baton Rouge township, where he was born April 6, 1829. He made good use of the common school educational advantages afforded him. Enlisting in the service of his country in the war of 1861-'65, in company F. Sixth regiment, he did his full duty to the close of the struggle. He served efficiently as a member of the legislature in 1888-'91. Zealous in the cause of agricultural education and development, he was elected in 1889 a member of the board of trustees of Clemson college and so continued until his death, attending every meeting when not prevented by sickness. He is survived by the following children: W. A. and T. H. Hardin, Mrs. Jessie L. Oates, Mrs. J. H. Yarborough and Miss Hattie Hardin, and a sister, Mrs. Anne Minter. His wife and two children, Mrs. W. A. Sanders of Chester, and J. Smith Hardin of Columbia, having predeceased him. Mr. Hardin was from early life a member of the Baptist church and was ever earnest and active in work for the welfare of his church.

— Lancaster special of August 27 to the Columbia State: The county campaign, which has been more or less hot since the opening nearly two weeks ago, reached the sizzling point at the meeting last night at the cotton mills, serious trouble being narrowly averted. At the conclusion of, Senator T. Y. Williams' speech, Representative J. Harry Foster gave the lie to Representative Harry Hines, both of whom were on the speakers' stand, the porch of the mill office being used as the rostrum. In an instant everything was in confusion. Men were crowding up on the porch, some were crying out, "Hit him, Harry!" and others, "Hit him, Hines!" Among those who got on the porch was Chief of Police H. N. Sowell, to whom Senator Williams remarked that he had no authority there, the meeting being outside the corporate limits. Mr. Sowell, replied that he was nevertheless a man, at the same time placing his hand on Mr. Williams. Parties rushed between the two determined men and bore them away from each other. For a few moments the excitement was intense. Had a single blow been struck or a shot fired, either on the stand or out in the swaying, excited crowd, there would no doubt have been much bloodshed and probably several fatalities. The paramount issue in the campaign, as heretofore published, is as to the justice or injustice of the levies made by the legislature for the Camden-Charlotte road and for permanent bridges thereon. Senator Williams and Representative Foster are upholding the levies, while Representative Hines is opposing them—and it was over some feature of this road question that the trouble started last night. Mr. Sowell resigned this morning the position of chief of police. The candidates spoke here today, and there was a large crowd in town.

— Anderson, August 27: Tom Leverett, who bears the reputation of being the meanest negro in Anderson county, especially when drinking, was shot and instantly killed by Chief of Police Murphy and Patrolman Shirley this afternoon on five o'clock when they attempted to arrest him for drinking and creating a disturbance. The officers in response to a police call went to Quince Leverett's blacksmith shop, one block from the city hall, and found that Tom Leverett had secreted himself, well armed, in a closet on the second floor of the shop. The officers several times called upon him to surrender and in reply he opened the door of the closet slightly and with terrible oaths attempted to draw his pistol on the officers. The officers each time pushed the door closed and would call upon him to drop his gun. Leverett refused to obey and said with oaths that he expected to fire if given an opportunity. When the door was opened again Leverett threw his pistol directly in Officer Shirley's face and then Chief Murphy and Officer Shirley opened fire, the shots being fired through a wooden partition. Only Leverett's hand and his pistol were in view. Several shots were fired and Leverett was heard to fall against the wall of the closet. One of the officers then attempted to open the door and Leverett was in a crouching position with his pistol ready to fire on the officers. Other shots were made and Leverett fell, death coming almost instantly. When moved to the morgue after being view by the coroner Leverett's body showed that eight shots had taken effect, three in the stomach and one in the head, hand, elbow, thigh and hip. Dr. Sanders says that the bullet that pierced his head is the one that caused death but the other shots would probably have proven fatal. Leverett has been drinking hard since yesterday and this afternoon before the shooting he was on the sidewalk near where the homicide occurred, waving his pistol in the air and cursing loudly. He has frequently been in trouble. The last serious trouble was shooting his wife and for this act there is an indictment now in the court of sessions. His reputation is of the worst. The coroner's inquest is being held tonight and a complete exoneration of the officers is expected just as soon as all the testimony of witnesses is in. The inquest is still going on at 10.30 tonight.

NEGRO DESPERADO KILLED.
Dqfied Arrest and is Shot to Death. Eight Wounds Inflicted.
Anderson, Aug. 27. — Tom Leverett, who bears the reputation of being the worst negro in Anderson county, especially when drinking, was shot and instantly killed by Chief of Police Murphy and Patrolman Shirley this afternoon when they attempted to arrest him for drinking and creating a disturbance.

The officers, in response to a police call, went to Quince Leverett's blacksmith shop and found that Tom Leverett had secreted himself, well armed, in a closet on the second floor of the shop. The officers several times called upon him to surrender. Leverett refused to obey, and said with oaths that he expected to fire if given an opportunity. When the door was opened Leverett threw his pistol directly in Officer Shirley's face and Chief Murphy and Officer Shirley opened fire, the shots being fired through a wooden partition. Only Leverett's hand and his pistol were in view.

Several shots were fired and Leverett was heard to fall against the wall of the closet. One of the officers then attempted to open the door. Leverett was in a crouching position with his pistol ready to fire. Other shots were made and Leverett fell. Death came almost instantly.

When moved to the morgue, after being viewed by the coroner, Leverett's body showed that eight shots had taken effect, three in the stomach, one each in the head, hand, elbow, thigh and hip. Dr. Sanders says that the bullet that pierced his head is what caused death, but the other shots would probably have proved fatal.
Leverett had been drinking hard since yesterday and this afternoon before the shooting he was on the sidewalk near where the homicide occurred waving his pistol in the air and cursing loudly.
He had frequently been in trouble. The last serious trouble was the shooting of his wife, and for this act there is an indictment now in the court of sessions. His reputation is of the worst.

POLICEMAN VINDICATED.
Trial In Anderson Results In Prompt Acquittal.
The case of the State vs. former Chief of Police L. M. Murphy and Officer J. C. Shirley, on trial for the killing of Tom Leverett, colored, a few weeks ago, ended rather abruptly yesterday afternoon, Judge Gary instructing the foreman of the jury to write a verdict of not guilty. Only about half the witnesses had been examined and Mr. W. B. King, Jr., had just left the stand.

Mr. G. C. Sullivan of counsel for the defense made a motion that the judge direct a verdict of not guilty, stating that the defense had numerous other witnesses but did not care to consume the time of the court unnecessarily.

Judge Gary asked Solicitor Bonham if he had any further testimony for the State, and the solicitor replied that he had not, and, on the motion, said that if his honor could not sustain the legal position, that this arrest could not be made without a warrant, of course, he could not ask for a verdict.

The judge replied: "I can't go that far. I think the officers were in the discharge of their duty. The negro defied arrest. He ought to have submitted. He knew the officers were policemen; they were in uniform and were in pursuit of the negro, who had just committed a serious breach of the peace by cursing on the street and brandishing his pistol.

"When the officers went to arrest the negro, he still had a pistol. The officers knew he was a dangerous man; had had trouble with him a number of times, in attempting to arrest him when drinking.
"I can't say that the officers did wrong. They had the right to make the arrest; it was their duty to do so, and to overcome the negro's resistance, even to taking his life.
"Even if the jury found a verdict, I could not sentence them.
"So I don't think we ought to take up more time in this case.
"Mr. Foreman, write a verdict of not guilty."
The case ended just as had been expected, and meets with general approval.—Anderson Mail.
